title: Letting Go of Abandoning Ourselves
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer uses her birthday as a prompt to argue that leaders, especially those not automatically welcomed into power structures, often protect themselves by withholding voice and presence until protection becomes self-abandonment. She separates boundaries, which express self-respect and preserve energy, from withdrawal, which severs connection and leaves harmful structures unchallenged. Her claim is that reclaiming power means returning to oneself and choosing authenticity over armor, not pursuing domination or visibility. The remedy is modest: small acts of kindness, honest conversations and letting oneself be seen. The post closes with reflection questions that help the reader tell a protective boundary from a diminishing retreat. It is a personal, reflective piece on leadership presence and character rather than a technique guide.
points: Self-protection through staying small or unseen gradually turns into self-abandonment.
A boundary clarifies what is yours to hold, while withdrawal severs connection to yourself and others.
Disengaging from systems you critique often reinforces them, because absence offers no alternative.
Reclaiming power comes through authenticity and presence, not domination or visibility for its own sake.
Re-entry shows up in small acts such as honest conversations and letting yourself be seen, not grand gestures.
quotes: There is an important distinction here: boundaries are an expression of self-respect. They clarify what is ours to hold and what is not. Withdrawal, on the other hand, severs connection to ourselves, to one another, and to the shared work of shaping a humane world.
We soften our voices. We hide parts of ourselves. We twist and contort in hopes of securing safety, prosperity, or belonging.
It quietly reinforces the very structures we critique by leaving them unchallenged, unquestioned, and unchanged. Absence creates no alternative.

And more personally, when we hide, cower, or make ourselves unrecognizable in the name of safety, we forfeit the very thing that actually sustains us: our innate knowing. Our presence. Our capacity to contribute the singular Gift only we can offer.
This is not a call to overexpose yourself or to force participation where it is not aligned. It is a gentle invitation back into presence.
We do not reclaim our power through domination or visibility for its own sake. We reclaim it by returning to ourselves, by choosing authenticity over armor.
